# The bake-off: six ways to make a decision {#sec-ch10}

In every team that makes many decisions, there is a long-running debate. The senior expert says the hand-written rules are enough, because anyone can read them. The data scientist says a trained model would do better, if someone labels enough data. The new engineer says an LLM understands cases better than both. And now someone has read about Jev. Each of them is right about something, because each is looking at a different quality. So let us put all the numbers on one page: six methods, one decision, one fair comparison. A comparison like this, where everyone makes the same thing, is sometimes called a "bake-off".

::: {.goals}
- Compare six ways of making the same decision.
- Judge methods on more than accuracy.
- Choose a method using a scorecard.
:::

## The six methods

![The six contestants: what each one reads, what it returns, and what it needs before it can start.](/figures/ch20/contenders.pdf){#fig-contenders}

The decision is: *is this alert a real attack?* Every method gets three weeks of labelled history ({{< num ch20 n_hist int >}} alerts) to learn from, and is then tested on a fourth week it has never seen ({{< num ch20 n_live int >}} alerts, of which {{< num ch20 live_threats int >}} are real attacks). The six methods are shown in @fig-contenders:

- hand-written **rules**;
- **logistic regression** on the alert's clean data fields;
- a simple **text classifier** that counts words in the raw text;
- an **LLM** asked to answer in a fixed format;
- an **LLM as judge**, giving each alert a rating from 1 to 10;
- **Jev**, reading the clean data fields.

An important note: the numbers for the LLM and for Jev in this comparison are illustrative examples, not measurements of the real products, and the example LLM was set up to read alerts less accurately. So if the LLM ranks below Jev, do not take that as proof about the real models. What you *can* rely on are the patterns that come from how each *type* of method works: how written confidences behave, how often text answers break, what happens when you ask twice, and what labels cost.

## The results

![Three views of how well each method separates threats from harmless alerts, on the live week. Left: ranking quality (AUC). Middle: the share of all real threats found if the team reviews the top 240 alerts each day. Right: calibration error, where lower is better.](/figures/ch20/scores.pdf){#fig-scores}

**Ranking.** Logistic regression wins, by a small margin: AUC {{< num ch20 logistic_auc f3 >}} against Jev's {{< num ch20 jev_auc f3 >}} (@fig-scores). This is not luck. It was trained on fifteen thousand of this company's own labelled alerts, with clean data, for a decision that depends on that data in a fairly simple way. This is exactly where classic machine learning is strongest. Rules come last ({{< num ch20 rules_auc f2 >}}): a rule only says yes or no, so it cannot tell which of its many "yes" cases to check first.

**Calibration.** Most methods are close to the diagonal. The LLM methods are not. The LLM's *written* confidence used only {{< num ch20 conf_levels int >}} different values across five thousand alerts, mostly 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99. A number that a model writes is just text, and text prefers round numbers. The LLM-as-judge rating from 1 to 10, when read as a probability, has the worst calibration of all ({{< num ch20 llm_judge_ece f3 >}}).

**Labels needed.** Logistic regression needs about 3,000 labelled cases to catch up with Jev, which needs none to start. A team with months of history has these labels. A new team, or a completely new decision, does not.

![Ranking on the live week as the trained methods see more labelled alerts, averaged over random samples. Jev and the LLMs need no labels to start, so they're flat lines. Logistic regression catches up with Jev at about 3,000 labels.](/figures/ch20/labels.pdf){#fig-labels}

::: {.keyidea}
**Labels are the hidden cost of trained models.** A trained model can win, but only after thousands of checked cases. A model that needs no labels can start today.
:::

**Speed and price.** Nothing is faster or cheaper than a rule, and classic models are close behind: they take millionths of a second on computers you already have. Jev's figures, as reported by the company, are in between: about \${{< num ch20 jev_cost_m int >}} per million decisions. The example LLM costs about \${{< num ch20 llm_json_cost_m int >}} per million (a little more than in Chapter 7, because here it also writes a short answer with a confidence) and takes about {{< num ch20 llm_json_latency f1 >}} seconds per answer.

![Time and cost per decision for each method, on log scales. Classic models run in millionths of a second, for fractions of a cent per million decisions (an assumption: computing cost only). The LLM figures are this book's illustrative assumptions; Jev's are vendor-reported.](/figures/ch20/cost-latency.pdf){#fig-cost-latency}

::: {.keyidea}
**If a simple rule or logistic regression works, use it.** It is faster, cheaper and easier to explain than any large model.
:::

Jev's price advantage is only against LLMs, not against everything.

**Stability.** When the same question was asked to the LLM five times, {{< num ch20 flip_rate pct1 >}} of the answers changed at least once, and {{< num ch20 parse_fail pct1 >}} of its answers could not be read by the program at all. Answers in a fixed typed shape cannot break like this.

## The scorecard

::: {.wide}
![The whole contest on one page. Bold marks the best in each numeric column. Every accuracy number is synthetic; every cost and time is an assumption, an illustration, or vendor-reported, as marked.](/figures/ch20/scorecard.pdf){#fig-scorecard-13}
:::

Read @fig-scorecard-13 column by column, and ask which columns matter for *your* decision.

- Thousands of labelled cases, clean data and a stable decision: logistic regression is hard to beat.
- Every decision must be explained to an auditor: rules are the clear winner.
- No labelled cases, raw text, or many different decisions: a System One model is the strongest choice, after a calibration check.
- The LLM is the weakest at deciding here, but it can do something no other method can: read anything, and *write*. Chapter 12 gives it exactly that job.

::: {.keyidea}
**There is no best method, only the best method for this decision.** Compare methods on ranking, calibration, labels needed, cost, speed and stability.
:::

::: {.breaks}
This is one decision in one example company, with illustrative numbers for the LLM and Jev. The test week has only about four hundred real attacks, so small differences in AUC may be due to chance. The real value of a bake-off is the *method*: run the same comparison on your own data, with the real models.
:::

::: {.threshold}
A new team will handle cloud storage alerts, a decision nobody has labelled yet. They will get about 300 labelled cases per week. Which method should they start with, and when should they reconsider?

(Start with a method that needs no labels. Use the first 300 labelled cases to check and fix its calibration. After a few weeks, train a logistic regression next to it. If both agree, keep the cheaper one. If they disagree, study the cases where they disagree.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Make a scorecard for a decision in your own work. Which three columns matter most?
:::
